title: The end of the beginning
pull: Not even the beginning of the end
quote: Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.
quoteBy: Winston Churchill, Lord Mayor's Day Luncheon, Mansion House, London, 10 November 1942

facts.text: On 10 November 1942, Prime Minister Winston Churchill spoke at the Lord Mayor's Day Luncheon at the Mansion House in London.
Britain had just won in Egypt. Churchill told the guests that Rommel's army had been defeated, routed, and very largely destroyed as a fighting force at El Alamein.
He credited General Alexander and his 'brilliant comrade and lieutenant, General Montgomery,' and said the fight should be called the Battle of Egypt.
Two days earlier, on 8 November, American and British troops had landed in French North Africa in Operation Torch.
Then came the famous lines, verbatim: 'Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.'
He went on to warn that from then on Hitler's Nazis would meet equally well armed, and perhaps better armed, troops.
Churchill's typed speaking notes survive, and the Imperial War Museums points to a single word he moved by hand to set the rhythm of the line.
The speech is listed as 'The Bright Gleam of Victory', and Churchill's notes are in his papers at the Churchill Archives Centre in Cambridge.

declassified.fact: In the same speech Churchill made it plain he would not give up the British Empire: 'I have not become the King's First Minister in order to preside over the liquidation of the British Empire.'

body:
Britain had just won in the desert, and Churchill refused to oversell it. One word in the line he chose, he had moved by hand.

10 November 1942. At the Lord Mayor's Day Luncheon at the Mansion House in London, Winston Churchill told the guests that Rommel's army had been defeated, routed, and very largely destroyed at El Alamein. Two days earlier, American and British troops had landed in French North Africa.

Then came the famous lines:

"Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning."

His typed speaking notes survive, and the Imperial War Museums points to the single word he moved to set the rhythm of the line.
